comments.text:
And here we are, less than 3 years later, and Brightline has filed for Bankruptcy.

I like Wendover but I hope people don't consider them to be reliable researchers. Brightline was doomed well before they made this video, and they ignored all the signs that industry experts were pointing to the whole time.

replies.author: @davidbova1759
replies.text: Early Bond Market Analysts: When the company (then called All Aboard Florida) first attempted to sell unrated bonds to finance construction in 2015 and 2017, they faced significant pushback from the high-yield debt market. Financial analysts at the time noted that taking on billions in debt for an unproven, private passenger rail startup was exceptionally risky, pointing out that virtually no private passenger rail service in the modern era had survived without heavy public subsidies.

replies.author: @davidbova1759
replies.text: Citizens Against Rail Expansion in Florida (CARE FL): Formed around 2014, this coalition of residents and local government officials from Florida's Treasure Coast (including Martin and Indian River counties) fought the project's funding for years. In federal lawsuits and congressional hearings between 2015 and 2018, CARE FL explicitly argued that Brightline's financial models were unviable and challenged the company's right to use tax-exempt private activity bonds to fund what they viewed as an incredibly risky venture.

replies.author: @davidbova1759
replies.text: Randal O'Toole (Cato Institute): A transportation policy analyst and senior fellow at the Cato Institute, O'Toole was a consistent and vocal skeptic of Brightline. In policy papers dating back to 2021 and earlier, he repeatedly warned that passenger rail cannot cover its capital costs without massive government subsidies. He argued that Brightline's ridership projections were highly inflated and suggested the project was essentially a real estate play that would fail as a standalone transportation business.

comments.author: @TheBlueprint89
comments.text: The untold half of the Brightline story is that it's a real-estate company that happens to run trains. Fortress bought the Florida East Coast corridor not just for the farebox but for the station-adjacent development rights — the railway turns those parcels into premium transit-oriented assets, and the land value uplift is where the equity return actually lives. Compare that to publicly funded HSR, where the uplift leaks out for free to surrounding landowners while taxpayers eat the construction risk. Whoever captures the land value captures the profit.
